---
title: "How do you name something new by its neighbours?"
subtitle: "You will do it by hand first, then teach it to a computer. All you need is arithmetic."
engine: knitr
---

Here are 29 plants of two kinds. Each one is a point, placed by two numbers: how long its leaves are, and how wide. Someone who knows plants has already marked each one as a circle or a cross.

A new plant arrives with no mark. You have to say which kind it is. Nobody has given you a rule. You are going to find that you already have one.

## What would you call this new plant?

The new plant is the ringed point with a question mark. Drag it anywhere you like. Then, before reading on, press *a circle* or *a cross* to say what you think it is.

::: {.ink-figure data-figure="neighbours-lab" data-step="0" data-caption="Fig. 1 · 29 made-up plants of two kinds, and a new one for you to name"}
:::

That was quick, and you did not do any sums. You looked at the plants around the question mark and went with what most of them were.

### Now tell a computer

A computer cannot look at a picture. It needs the plants as numbers. Each one is a pair, such as `(3.4, 3.9)`: 3.4 across and 3.9 up. The kinds are numbers too: 0 for a circle, 1 for a cross. The cell below fetches the same 29 plants, their kinds, and the new plant where you left it.

Press **Run**. The first time takes a few seconds while Python starts.

::: {.py-cell data-draw="py-plot"}
```python
from page import points, kinds, new_point    # the plants above, their kinds, and your new plant

print("There are", len(points), "plants.")
print("The first is", points[0], "and its kind is", kinds[0])
print("The new plant is at", new_point)

picture = {"points": points, "labels": kinds, "stars": [new_point],
           "xlabel": "leaf length", "ylabel": "leaf width"}
```
:::

`print` writes its words and numbers out, and `len` counts how many things a list holds. `points[0]` is the first plant in the list: counting starts at 0. The last lines leave a `picture` behind, and the page draws it under the cell from your code's own numbers.

## Who did you look at?

You did not look at all 29. Plants far away, in a corner, told you nothing about the new one. You looked at the few closest to it.

::: {.ink-figure data-figure="neighbours-lab" data-step="1" data-caption="Fig. 2 · threads from the new plant to its nearest few, and their vote"}
:::

Threads run from the new plant to its 5 nearest neighbours, nearest first. The dotted circle reaches as far as the fifth: everything inside it is nearer than that. Each neighbour gets one vote for its own kind, and the kind with more votes wins.

That is the whole rule: **look at the few known points nearest to the new one, and go with the majority.**

Now move the slider. With 1 neighbour, only the very nearest plant decides. With the plant where it starts, that nearest one is a stray cross sitting among the circles, so the answer flips to *cross*. Drag the new plant around too, and watch which threads change.

The slider only stops at odd numbers. With two kinds and an odd number of votes, one kind always has more, so there is never a tie.

## How far is each plant from the new one?

"Nearest" means measuring distance, so that comes first. Try one by hand. The new plant starts at (4.4, 3.6). The stray cross is at (5.1, 3.5). It is 0.7 across and 0.1 down.

Multiply each by itself and add: 0.7 × 0.7 = 0.49, and 0.1 × 0.1 = 0.01, and 0.49 + 0.01 = **0.5**. That is the squared distance. Up or down makes no difference: a number times itself is never negative. The circle at (3.4, 3.9) is 1.0 across and 0.3 up: 1.0 × 1.0 = 1.0, and 0.3 × 0.3 = 0.09, so **1.09**. The cross is nearer.

You never need the true distance, only which is smaller. Squaring keeps the order, so the squared distance will do.

The code below does the same sum. One piece is missing. Replace the blank and press Run.

::: {.py-cell}
```python
def dist2(p, q):
    across = p[0] - q[0]          # p[0] is the first number of the pair
    up = p[1] - q[1]              # p[1] is the second
    return across * across + ____

print(dist2((0, 0), (3, 4)))                        # 3 across and 4 up: 9 + 16 is 25
print(round(dist2((4.4, 3.6), (5.1, 3.5)), 2))     # by hand this was 0.5
```
::: {.py-solution}
```python
def dist2(p, q):
    across = p[0] - q[0]          # p[0] is the first number of the pair
    up = p[1] - q[1]              # p[1] is the second
    return across * across + up * up

print(dist2((0, 0), (3, 4)))                        # 3 across and 4 up: 9 + 16 is 25
print(round(dist2((4.4, 3.6), (5.1, 3.5)), 2))     # by hand this was 0.5
```
:::
:::

`def` gives a set of steps a name, so you can use them again, and `return` hands back the answer. From now on, `dist2(a, b)` means "do that sum for a and b". `round(x, 2)` keeps two decimals, because a computer works out 0.7 × 0.7 as 0.48999999999999994.

Now measure from the new plant to every one of the 29. A list can start empty, `[]`, and grow: `append` puts one more thing on its end. `for p in points` takes each plant in turn.

::: {.py-cell data-draw="py-plot"}
```python
def distances(q, points):
    out = []                                  # an empty list, to fill in
    for p in points:                          # take each known plant in turn
        out.append(dist2(q, p))               # put its distance on the end
    return out

dists = distances(new_point, points)
print(len(dists), "distances. The first five:")
for i in range(5):                            # i is 0, 1, 2, 3, 4
    print("plant", i, "at", points[i], "is", round(dists[i], 2), "away")

# the picture: one more thread each time round
frames = []
threads = []
for p in points:
    threads.append((new_point, p))
    frames.append({"points": points, "labels": kinds, "stars": [new_point],
                   "segments": list(threads)})          # list(...) makes a copy of the threads so far
```
:::

The picture plays back the loop: one thread for every plant, 29 in all. The computer measures them all. It has no way to know which are close until it has measured every one.

## Which few are nearest?

By hand, you would find the smallest distance and tick that plant. Then you would find the smallest of the ones left, and tick that. Five times, for five neighbours.

::: {.ask}
When the code below finishes, how would you know it picked the right five?

- **Check that it printed five plants.** That only shows it picked five. They could be the wrong five.
- **Check that the distances it prints are small.** Small compared with what? Without the other 24 to compare, you cannot tell.
- **Compare with Fig. 2.** Yes. Set the slider there to 5 and leave the new plant where it is. You picked the same plants by eye. The plants the code prints should be the ones at the end of the threads.
:::

The code below is that ticking, written out. `chosen` is the list of plants ticked so far. `best` is the nearest one found so far in this round; it starts as `None`, Python's word for "nothing yet". `i in chosen` asks whether plant `i` is already ticked, and `if` runs the lines under it only when its test is true.

::: {.py-cell data-draw="py-plot"}
```python
def nearest_few(dists, k):
    chosen = []                                       # plants ticked so far
    for pick in range(k):                             # k rounds, one tick each
        best = None                                   # nothing found yet this round
        for i in range(len(dists)):                   # look at every plant
            if i not in chosen:                       # skip the ones already ticked
                if best is None or dists[i] < dists[best]:
                    best = ____                       # nearer than any so far: remember which
        chosen.append(best)
    return chosen

near = nearest_few(dists, 5)
for i in near:
    print("plant", i, "at", points[i], "kind", kinds[i], "distance", round(dists[i], 2))

# the picture: one thread for each tick
frames = []
threads = []
for i in near:
    threads.append((new_point, points[i]))
    frames.append({"points": points, "labels": kinds, "stars": [new_point], "segments": list(threads)})
```
::: {.py-solution}
```python

        for i in range(len(dists)):                   # look at every plant
            if i not in chosen:                       # skip the ones already ticked
                if best is None or dists[i] < dists[best]:

        chosen.append(best)
    return chosen

near = nearest_few(dists, 5)
for i in near:

# the picture: one thread for each tick
```

:::

Watch the margin of the cell as it runs: the line that looks at every plant runs 29 times in each of the 5 rounds. The picture adds the threads in the order they were ticked, nearest first, just as Fig. 2 sewed them.

## Who wins the vote?

Now count. Each of the nearest few adds one vote to its own kind. `counts` holds two tallies: `counts[0]` for circles and `counts[1]` for crosses. One blank is left: what should the crosses beat?

::: {.py-cell data-draw="py-plot"}
```python
names = ["circle", "cross"]                           # names[0] is "circle", names[1] is "cross"

def vote(q, points, kinds, k):
    near = nearest_few(distances(q, points), k)
    counts = [0, 0]                                   # votes for circles, votes for crosses
    for i in near:
        counts[kinds[i]] = counts[kinds[i]] + 1       # one more vote for this plant's kind
    if counts[1] > ____:                              # more crosses than circles?
        return 1, near, counts
    return 0, near, counts

answer, near, counts = vote(new_point, points, kinds, 5)
print("Votes:", counts[0], "circles,", counts[1], "crosses. It is a", names[answer])

threads = []
for i in near:
    threads.append((new_point, points[i]))
picture = {"points": points, "labels": kinds, "stars": [new_point], "segments": threads,
           "notes": [str(counts[0]) + " circles", str(counts[1]) + " crosses", "says: " + names[answer]]}
```
::: {.py-solution}
```python
names = ["circle", "cross"]                           # names[0] is "circle", names[1] is "cross"

def vote(q, points, kinds, k):
    near = nearest_few(distances(q, points), k)
    counts = [0, 0]                                   # votes for circles, votes for crosses
    for i in near:
        counts[kinds[i]] = counts[kinds[i]] + 1       # one more vote for this plant's kind
    if counts[1] > counts[0]:                         # more crosses than circles?
        return 1, near, counts
    return 0, near, counts

answer, near, counts = vote(new_point, points, kinds, 5)
print("Votes:", counts[0], "circles,", counts[1], "crosses. It is a", names[answer])

threads = []
for i in near:
    threads.append((new_point, points[i]))
picture = {"points": points, "labels": kinds, "stars": [new_point], "segments": threads,
           "notes": [str(counts[0]) + " circles", str(counts[1]) + " crosses", "says: " + names[answer]]}
```
:::
:::

A function can hand back several things at once: `vote` returns the answer, the neighbours and the tallies, and the line under it catches all three. Compare the vote it prints with Fig. 2 with the slider at 5. Same plants, same new plant, same rule: they should agree. Change the 5 in the code to 1 and run it again. It should flip, just as the slider did.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="The same thing in symbols"}
For two points $p$ and $q$, each with two numbers, the squared distance is

$$d^2(p, q) = (p_1 - q_1)^2 + (p_2 - q_2)^2$$

With more measurements you add one more square for each. The ordinary distance is the square root of this, $\sqrt{3^2 + 4^2} = 5$, and it puts the points in the same order. Other rulers exist. Adding the gaps without squaring them, $|p_1 - q_1| + |p_2 - q_2|$, measures as if walking along a street grid. For yes-or-no measurements, people count how many of them differ.

With $N_k(x)$ for the $k$ known points nearest to a new point $x$, and $y_i$ for the kind of point $i$, the answer is

$$\hat{y} = \text{the most common } y_i \text{ among the points in } N_k(x)$$

Read $\hat{y}$ as "the guess for y". If $k$ is even, the vote can tie. Use an odd $k$, break the tie at random, or let nearer neighbours count for more.
:::

## How many neighbours should vote?

Five was handed to you. Nothing says it must be five.

::: {.ask data-veil="true"}
What happens if only 1 neighbour votes? And if all 29 do?

- **One is best: the nearest plant is the most like the new one.** It is the most alike, and that is the trouble. If the nearest plant is a stray, the answer is a stray too.
- **All 29 is best: more opinions are safer.** With all 29 voting, the answer is the same everywhere: whichever kind has more plants. There are 16 circles and 13 crosses, so everything becomes a circle.
- **Somewhere in between.** Yes. Too few and one odd plant decides. Too many and the plants far away outvote the ones nearby.
:::

::: {.ink-figure data-figure="neighbours-lab" data-step="2" data-caption="Fig. 3 · the vote at every spot on the page: hatched where crosses win"}
:::

This picture asks the vote at every spot on the page, not just at your new plant. The line is the border, where the vote tips from one kind to the other. Press *slide from 1 to 29* and watch it.

At 1, the border bends around every stray plant and gives each one its own island. It would be different with a different 29 plants. Between about 5 and 15 it settles into a calmer line between the two groups. Near 29, the border has nowhere left to go: the bigger group wins everywhere.

No sum tells you the best number. You try a few, test each one on plants whose kind you know but kept back, and keep the number that names them best. A later lesson, *Testing on unseen data*, shows how. Until then, two habits help: use an odd number when there are two kinds, and start near the square root of how many points you have. For 29 plants that is about 5.

## What if one measurement is in big numbers?

Here is a new set of points: 28 people who asked a bank for a loan. Each is placed by their income, in dollars, and their credit score, a number from about 300 to 850 that says how reliably they have paid back before. Some were approved (+), some were turned down (o). A new person asks: income $62,000, score 720.

::: {.ask data-veil="true"}
Which of the two measurements will decide who counts as nearest?

- **Both, equally.** They are both in the sum. But look at the sizes. A gap of $2,000 in income adds 2,000 × 2,000 = 4,000,000. A gap of 200 in score, nearly the whole range, adds 200 × 200 = 40,000.
- **The income.** Yes. Its numbers are in thousands, so its gaps swamp everything else. The score barely counts.
- **The credit score.** It says much more about paying back, so you would hope so. But the sum does not know that. It only sees numbers, and the income numbers are far bigger.
:::

::: {.ink-figure data-figure="knn-scale-figure" data-step="2" data-caption="Fig. 4 · 28 made-up loan applicants, the new one (the square), and its 5 nearest. The slider sets how much income counts"}
:::

The slider starts where the sum leaves it: income in dollars, score in points. The hatched strip is every spot as near as the fifth neighbour. It is a thin upright strip, so the "nearest" five are just the five with the closest incomes, wherever their scores are. Four were turned down, so the vote says *deny*. The *income share* says how much of the distance comes from income: nearly all of it. The number by the slider says how many times more income counts here than it will once both are scaled: about 257 times.

Now drag the slider to the left, toward *scaled*, so income counts less. The strip widens into a circle and takes in people whose income and score are both like the new person's. All five were approved. Same people, same new person, same rule. Only the units changed, and with them the answer.

### How does it break?

Here is the same thing in code. The cell fetches the 28 applicants and runs your `vote` on the raw numbers, as they come.

::: {.py-cell data-draw="py-plot" data-aside="true"}
```python
from page import applicants, approved, applicant    # (income, score) pairs, 1 or 0, and the new person

answer, near, counts = vote(applicant, applicants, approved, 5)
for i in near:
    print("income", applicants[i][0], " score", applicants[i][1], " approved:", approved[i])
print("Votes:", counts[0], "deny,", counts[1], "approve")

threads = []
for i in near:
    threads.append((applicant, applicants[i]))
picture = {"points": applicants, "labels": approved, "stars": [applicant], "segments": threads,
           "xlabel": "income", "ylabel": "score", "notes": ["raw units", str(counts[1]) + " of 5 approve"]}
```
:::

Nothing goes wrong that Python can see. It runs, and it prints an answer. Look at the five it chose: every income is within $3,000 of $62,000, and the scores run all the way from 614 to 713. Four of the five have scores well below the new person's 720. The code has quietly ignored the score. That is the worst kind of break: a wrong answer that looks like a right one.

::: {.ask}
What should you do about it?

- **Leave the income out.** Then the score decides alone. That is the same mistake the other way round, and it throws away something that matters.
- **Use more neighbours.** The neighbours would still be picked by income, just more of them. The trouble is the ruler, not the count.
- **Put both on the same footing first.** Yes. Measure each one in steps of its own typical spread, so a usual gap in income and a usual gap in score count the same.
:::

The fix is two small steps for each measurement. Take away its average, so the middle sits at 0. Then divide by its spread, the typical distance from that average. Incomes here average about $61,000, with a spread of about $16,000. So an income of $69,000 becomes (69,000 − 61,000) ÷ 16,000 = 0.5: half a typical step above the middle. Scores average about 661 with a spread of about 63, so the new person's 720 becomes (720 − 661) ÷ 63, a little under 1. Scores get the same treatment with their own average and spread. After that, a 1 in income and a 1 in score mean the same thing: one typical step.

`sum` adds up a list. `math.sqrt` is the square root, which undoes a square: `math.sqrt(25)` is 5. The new person is scaled with the same average and spread as everyone else. That is the blank.

::: {.py-cell data-draw="py-plot"}
```python
import math
from page import applicants, approved, applicant    # the same applicants as above

def average_and_spread(values):
    avg = sum(values) / len(values)                  # the average
    total = 0
    for v in values:
        total = total + (v - avg) * (v - avg)        # how far from the average, squared
    spread = math.sqrt(total / len(values))          # the typical distance from the average
    return avg, spread

incomes = []
scores = []
for p in applicants:
    incomes.append(p[0])
    scores.append(p[1])
avg_i, spread_i = average_and_spread(incomes)
avg_s, spread_s = average_and_spread(scores)
print("income: average", round(avg_i), " spread", round(spread_i))
print("score:  average", round(avg_s), " spread", round(spread_s))

scaled = []
for p in applicants:
    scaled.append(((p[0] - avg_i) / spread_i, (p[1] - avg_s) / spread_s))
new_scaled = ((applicant[0] - avg_i) / spread_i, ____)

answer, near, counts = vote(new_scaled, scaled, approved, 5)
print("Votes:", counts[0], "deny,", counts[1], "approve")

threads = []
for i in near:
    threads.append((new_scaled, scaled[i]))
picture = {"points": scaled, "labels": approved, "stars": [new_scaled], "segments": threads,
           "xlabel": "income, scaled", "ylabel": "score, scaled",
           "notes": ["scaled", str(counts[1]) + " of 5 approve"]}
```
::: {.py-solution}
```python
import math
from page import applicants, approved, applicant    # the same applicants as above

def average_and_spread(values):
    avg = sum(values) / len(values)                  # the average
    total = 0
    for v in values:
        total = total + (v - avg) * (v - avg)        # how far from the average, squared
    spread = math.sqrt(total / len(values))          # the typical distance from the average
    return avg, spread

incomes = []
scores = []
for p in applicants:
    incomes.append(p[0])
    scores.append(p[1])
avg_i, spread_i = average_and_spread(incomes)
avg_s, spread_s = average_and_spread(scores)
print("income: average", round(avg_i), " spread", round(spread_i))
print("score:  average", round(avg_s), " spread", round(spread_s))

scaled = []
for p in applicants:
    scaled.append(((p[0] - avg_i) / spread_i, (p[1] - avg_s) / spread_s))
new_scaled = ((applicant[0] - avg_i) / spread_i, (applicant[1] - avg_s) / spread_s)

answer, near, counts = vote(new_scaled, scaled, approved, 5)
print("Votes:", counts[0], "deny,", counts[1], "approve")

threads = []
for i in near:
    threads.append((new_scaled, scaled[i]))
picture = {"points": scaled, "labels": approved, "stars": [new_scaled], "segments": threads,
           "xlabel": "income, scaled", "ylabel": "score, scaled",
           "notes": ["scaled", str(counts[1]) + " of 5 approve"]}
```
:::
:::

Compare the vote with Fig. 4 with the slider all the way to *scaled*. Both should say 5 approve. Your `vote` did not change at all. Only the numbers you gave it did.

Any method that measures distance has this weakness, so scale first whenever the measurements come in different units.

## What else can it do, and what does it cost?

**It can predict a number, not just a kind.** Say each known point were a house, placed by its size and its distance from town, with the price it sold for. For a new house, find the nearest few and take the average of their prices instead of a vote. If the three nearest sold for 200, 240 and 220 thousand, the guess is (200 + 240 + 220) ÷ 3 = 220 thousand. How many to ask works the same way: 1 neighbour follows every odd sale, and all of them gives the same average price for every house.

**It does nothing until you ask, and then it does everything.** There is no step where it learns. It keeps every known point and, for each new question, measures the distance to all of them, just as your `distances` did. With 29 plants that is 29 sums. With a million known points and a thousand questions, it is a thousand million.

**It struggles with many measurements.** With two numbers per point, "nearest" means something. With hundreds, nearly every point ends up about as far from the new one as every other, and the nearest few are hardly nearer than the rest. A common cure is to boil the measurements down to a few first. A later lesson, *Reshaping data*, shows one way.

In return it is simple, it needs no guess about the shape of the groups, the border bends wherever the points send it, and it works the same for three or ten kinds: you just count more tallies.

## What you just built

Everything you did has a name:

| What you did | What it is called |
|:--|:--|
| Naming the kind of a new point from points whose kind you know | Classification |
| The plants whose kind you were told | Training data, with labels |
| Look at the nearest few, go with the majority | k nearest neighbours (KNN) |
| How many get a vote | *k* |
| Across times across, plus up times up | Squared Euclidean distance |
| The line on the map where the vote tips | The decision boundary |
| One voter, an island for every stray | Overfitting: too sensitive to the sample (high variance) |
| Everyone votes, the bigger group always wins | Underfitting: too blunt (high bias) |
| Taking away the average, dividing by the spread | Standardising, or z-scores (the spread is the standard deviation) |
| Averaging the neighbours' numbers instead of voting | KNN regression |
| Doing no work until a question arrives | A lazy learner |
| "Nearest" meaning less as measurements pile up | The curse of dimensionality |

You did not need the names to do it. A library such as scikit-learn has a `KNeighborsClassifier` that does exactly this: it stores the points, and when asked, finds the nearest *k* and counts. It does not scale the measurements for you, so that step is still yours. To save time on big data, it can file the points in a tree beforehand so it does not have to measure to every single one.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Reference: the same ideas in R"}
Every plot below is produced by the R on this page. Open "The R" under any of them to see the code.

Two groups of labelled points and one new point without a label.

```{r}
#| label: plot-mystery-point
#| fig-cap: "A new point (black diamond) arrives. Which group does it belong to?"

library(ggplot2)
set.seed(42)

df <- data.frame(
  x1 = c(rnorm(30, 2, 0.7), rnorm(30, 5, 0.7)),
  x2 = c(rnorm(30, 2, 0.7), rnorm(30, 5, 0.7)),
  group = factor(rep(c("Red", "Blue"), each = 30))
)

new_point <- data.frame(x1 = 3.8, x2 = 3.5)

ggplot(df, aes(x1, x2, color = group)) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  geom_point(data = new_point, aes(x1, x2), color = "black",
             shape = 18, size = 6, inherit.aes = FALSE) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("steelblue", "coral")) +
  annotate("text", x = 4.1, y = 3.2, label = "???", fontface = "bold", size = 5) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14) +
  labs(x = "Feature 1", y = "Feature 2")
```

The algorithm by hand for $k = 5$: every distance, the five smallest, the vote.

```{r}
#| label: plot-knn-step-by-step
#| fig-cap: "k=5: find 5 nearest neighbors, take majority vote"

# Calculate distances from new point to all training points
df$dist <- sqrt((df$x1 - new_point$x1)^2 + (df$x2 - new_point$x2)^2)
df$rank <- rank(df$dist)
df$is_neighbor <- df$rank <= 5

# Count votes
neighbors <- df[df$is_neighbor, ]
vote_red <- sum(neighbors$group == "Red")
vote_blue <- sum(neighbors$group == "Blue")

ggplot(df, aes(x1, x2, color = group)) +
  geom_point(size = 3, alpha = 0.3) +
  # Highlight neighbors
  geom_point(data = neighbors, aes(x1, x2, color = group), size = 4) +
  # Draw lines from new point to neighbors
  geom_segment(data = neighbors,
    aes(x = new_point$x1, y = new_point$x2, xend = x1, yend = x2),
    color = "gray50", linetype = "dashed", inherit.aes = FALSE) +
  # New point
  geom_point(data = new_point, aes(x1, x2), color = "black",
             shape = 18, size = 6, inherit.aes = FALSE) +
  # Circle around neighborhood
  annotate("path",
    x = new_point$x1 + max(neighbors$dist) * cos(seq(0, 2*pi, length.out = 100)),
    y = new_point$x2 + max(neighbors$dist) * sin(seq(0, 2*pi, length.out = 100)),
    linetype = "dotted", color = "gray40") +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("steelblue", "coral")) +
  annotate("label", x = 5.5, y = 1.5, size = 4,
    label = paste0("Vote: ", vote_red, " Red, ", vote_blue, " Blue\n",
                   "Winner: ", ifelse(vote_red > vote_blue, "Red", "Blue"))) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14) +
  labs(x = "Feature 1", y = "Feature 2")
```

Euclidean distance between two points is the hypotenuse of a right triangle.

```{r}
#| label: plot-distance-visual
#| fig-cap: "Euclidean distance = straight-line distance between two points"

p1 <- data.frame(x1 = 2, x2 = 1)
p2 <- data.frame(x1 = 5, x2 = 5)
d <- sqrt((p2$x1 - p1$x1)^2 + (p2$x2 - p1$x2)^2)

ggplot() +
  # The two points
  geom_point(data = p1, aes(x1, x2), size = 5, color = "coral") +
  geom_point(data = p2, aes(x1, x2), size = 5, color = "steelblue") +
  # Direct line (hypotenuse)
  geom_segment(aes(x = p1$x1, y = p1$x2, xend = p2$x1, yend = p2$x2),
               linewidth = 1.2) +
  # Horizontal leg
  geom_segment(aes(x = p1$x1, y = p1$x2, xend = p2$x1, yend = p1$x2),
               linetype = "dashed", color = "gray50") +
  # Vertical leg
  geom_segment(aes(x = p2$x1, y = p1$x2, xend = p2$x1, yend = p2$x2),
               linetype = "dashed", color = "gray50") +
  # Labels
  annotate("text", x = 3.5, y = 0.6, label = paste0("Δx₁ = ", p2$x1 - p1$x1), size = 4) +
  annotate("text", x = 5.5, y = 3, label = paste0("Δx₂ = ", p2$x2 - p1$x2), size = 4) +
  annotate("text", x = 3, y = 3.8,
    label = paste0("d = √(3² + 4²) = ", round(d, 1)), size = 4.5, fontface = "bold") +
  coord_equal() +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14) +
  labs(x = "Feature 1", y = "Feature 2")
```

The same new point at $k$ = 1, 3 and 7. The neighbourhood grows and the vote is recounted.

```{r}
#| label: plot-voting
#| fig-cap: "Different k values lead to different votes"

library(class)

# Show votes for k = 1, 3, 7
k_vals <- c(1, 3, 7)

par(mfrow = c(1, 3), mar = c(4, 4, 3, 1))

for (k in k_vals) {
  # Find neighbors
  nn <- df[order(df$dist)[1:k], ]
  vote_r <- sum(nn$group == "Red")
  vote_b <- sum(nn$group == "Blue")
  winner <- ifelse(vote_r > vote_b, "Red", "Blue")

  plot(df$x1, df$x2,
    col = ifelse(df$group == "Red", "coral", "steelblue"),
    pch = 19, cex = 1, main = paste0("k = ", k),
    xlab = "Feature 1", ylab = "Feature 2")

  # Circle neighbors
  points(nn$x1, nn$x2,
    col = ifelse(nn$group == "Red", "coral", "steelblue"),
    pch = 19, cex = 2)
  points(nn$x1, nn$x2, pch = 1, cex = 2.5, lwd = 2)

  # New point
  points(new_point$x1, new_point$x2, pch = 18, cex = 3, col = "black")

  # Draw radius
  radius <- max(nn$dist)
  theta <- seq(0, 2 * pi, length.out = 100)
  lines(new_point$x1 + radius * cos(theta),
        new_point$x2 + radius * sin(theta),
        lty = 3, col = "gray40")

  legend("topleft", bty = "n", cex = 0.9,
    legend = c(
      paste0("Red: ", vote_r, "  Blue: ", vote_b),
      paste0("→ ", winner)
    ))
}
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

The whole decision boundary at $k$ = 1, 5 and 25, from jagged to smooth.

```{r}
#| label: plot-k-boundaries
#| fig-cap: "Small k = jagged boundary (overfit). Large k = smooth boundary (underfit)."

# Full decision boundary comparison
grid <- expand.grid(
  x1 = seq(min(df$x1) - 0.5, max(df$x1) + 0.5, length.out = 150),
  x2 = seq(min(df$x2) - 0.5, max(df$x2) + 0.5, length.out = 150)
)

par(mfrow = c(1, 3), mar = c(4, 4, 3, 1))

for (k in c(1, 5, 25)) {
  pred <- knn(
    train = df[, c("x1", "x2")],
    test = grid[, c("x1", "x2")],
    cl = df$group,
    k = k
  )

  plot(df$x1, df$x2,
    col = ifelse(df$group == "Red", "coral", "steelblue"),
    pch = 19, cex = 1.2,
    main = paste("k =", k),
    xlab = "Feature 1", ylab = "Feature 2")

  points(grid$x1, grid$x2,
    col = ifelse(pred == "Red",
      adjustcolor("coral", 0.15),
      adjustcolor("steelblue", 0.15)),
    pch = 15, cex = 0.3)

  legend("topleft", bty = "n", cex = 0.9,
    legend = ifelse(k == 1, "Memorizes data (overfit)",
      ifelse(k >= 25, "Too smooth (underfit)", "Balanced")))
}
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

Income and credit score before and after standardising.

```{r}
#| label: plot-scaling
#| fig-cap: "Without scaling, income dominates. With scaling, both features contribute equally."

set.seed(7)

# Income: 30k-90k range. Credit score: 300-850 range.
df_raw <- data.frame(
  income = c(rnorm(40, 50000, 8000), rnorm(40, 70000, 8000)),
  credit = c(rnorm(40, 580, 40), rnorm(40, 720, 40)),
  group = factor(rep(c("Deny", "Approve"), each = 40))
)

par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 3, 1))

# Unscaled
plot(df_raw$income, df_raw$credit,
  col = ifelse(df_raw$group == "Deny", "coral", "steelblue"),
  pch = 19, main = "Unscaled",
  xlab = "Income ($)", ylab = "Credit Score")
mtext("Income range: 60,000\nCredit range: 500\nIncome dominates!",
      side = 1, line = -3, cex = 0.8, col = "red")

# Scaled
df_scaled <- df_raw
df_scaled$income <- scale(df_scaled$income)
df_scaled$credit <- scale(df_scaled$credit)

plot(df_scaled$income, df_scaled$credit,
  col = ifelse(df_scaled$group == "Deny", "coral", "steelblue"),
  pch = 19, main = "Scaled (standardized)",
  xlab = "Income (z-score)", ylab = "Credit Score (z-score)")
mtext("Both features: mean=0, sd=1\nEqual contribution to distance",
      side = 1, line = -3, cex = 0.8, col = "darkgreen")

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

KNN accuracy with $k = 5$ on the unscaled and the scaled features.

```{r}
#| label: plot-scaling-accuracy
#| fig-cap: "Scaling dramatically improves KNN accuracy when features have different ranges"

# Compare accuracy with and without scaling
acc_unscaled <- mean(
  knn(df_raw[, c("income", "credit")], df_raw[, c("income", "credit")],
      df_raw$group, k = 5) == df_raw$group
)

acc_scaled <- mean(
  knn(df_scaled[, c("income", "credit")], df_scaled[, c("income", "credit")],
      df_scaled$group, k = 5) == df_scaled$group
)

barplot(
  c(Unscaled = acc_unscaled, Scaled = acc_scaled) * 100,
  col = c("coral", "steelblue"),
  ylab = "Accuracy (%)", ylim = c(0, 100),
  main = "KNN (k=5) Accuracy: Scaled vs Unscaled"
)
abline(h = 50, lty = 2, col = "gray50")
text(0.7, 55, "Random guessing", col = "gray50", cex = 0.8)
```

KNN regression on a noisy sine curve at three values of $k$.

```{r}
#| label: plot-knn-regression
#| fig-cap: "KNN regression: predict by averaging the k nearest neighbors' values"

set.seed(12)
x <- sort(runif(50, 0, 10))
y <- sin(x) + rnorm(50, 0, 0.3)
df_reg <- data.frame(x = x, y = y)

# Predict for a grid of x values
x_grid <- seq(0, 10, length.out = 200)

par(mfrow = c(1, 3), mar = c(4, 4, 3, 1))

for (k in c(1, 5, 15)) {
  y_pred <- sapply(x_grid, function(xnew) {
    dists <- abs(df_reg$x - xnew)
    nn_idx <- order(dists)[1:k]
    mean(df_reg$y[nn_idx])
  })

  plot(df_reg$x, df_reg$y, pch = 19, col = "gray40",
    main = paste("KNN Regression: k =", k),
    xlab = "x", ylab = "y")
  lines(x_grid, y_pred, col = "steelblue", lwd = 2)
  lines(x_grid, sin(x_grid), col = "coral", lty = 2, lwd = 1.5)
  legend("topright", bty = "n", cex = 0.8,
    legend = c("KNN prediction", "True function"),
    col = c("steelblue", "coral"), lty = c(1, 2), lwd = 2)
}
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

The same overlapping data classified by a linear SVM and by KNN.

```{r}
#| label: plot-svm-vs-knn
#| fig-cap: "Same data, different approaches: SVM draws a boundary, KNN uses local voting"

library(e1071)

# Slightly overlapping data
set.seed(55)
df_cmp <- data.frame(
  x1 = c(rnorm(50, 2, 1), rnorm(50, 4.5, 1)),
  x2 = c(rnorm(50, 2, 1), rnorm(50, 4.5, 1)),
  group = factor(rep(c("A", "B"), each = 50))
)

grid_cmp <- expand.grid(
  x1 = seq(-1, 8, length.out = 150),
  x2 = seq(-1, 8, length.out = 150)
)

par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 3, 1))

# SVM
fit_svm <- svm(group ~ x1 + x2, data = df_cmp, kernel = "linear", cost = 1)
grid_cmp$svm_pred <- predict(fit_svm, grid_cmp)

plot(df_cmp$x1, df_cmp$x2,
  col = ifelse(df_cmp$group == "A", "steelblue", "coral"),
  pch = 19, cex = 1.2, main = "SVM (linear)",
  xlab = "Feature 1", ylab = "Feature 2")
points(grid_cmp$x1, grid_cmp$x2,
  col = ifelse(grid_cmp$svm_pred == "A",
    adjustcolor("steelblue", 0.15), adjustcolor("coral", 0.15)),
  pch = 15, cex = 0.3)
points(df_cmp$x1[fit_svm$index], df_cmp$x2[fit_svm$index],
  pch = 1, cex = 2.5, lwd = 2)
legend("topleft", bty = "n", legend = "○ = support vectors", cex = 0.8)

# KNN
knn_pred <- knn(
  train = df_cmp[, c("x1", "x2")],
  test = grid_cmp[, c("x1", "x2")],
  cl = df_cmp$group, k = 5
)

plot(df_cmp$x1, df_cmp$x2,
  col = ifelse(df_cmp$group == "A", "steelblue", "coral"),
  pch = 19, cex = 1.2, main = "KNN (k = 5)",
  xlab = "Feature 1", ylab = "Feature 2")
points(grid_cmp$x1, grid_cmp$x2,
  col = ifelse(knn_pred == "A",
    adjustcolor("steelblue", 0.15), adjustcolor("coral", 0.15)),
  pch = 15, cex = 0.3)
legend("topleft", bty = "n", legend = "No explicit boundary", cex = 0.8)

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

The ratio of the farthest to the nearest distance as the number of features grows.

```{r}
#| label: plot-curse
#| fig-cap: "In high dimensions, the gap between nearest and farthest neighbor shrinks"

set.seed(1)
dims <- c(2, 5, 10, 50, 100, 500)
ratios <- sapply(dims, function(d) {
  data <- matrix(rnorm(1000 * d), ncol = d)
  query <- rnorm(d)
  dists <- sqrt(rowSums((data - matrix(query, nrow = 1000, ncol = d, byrow = TRUE))^2))
  max(dists) / min(dists)
})

barplot(ratios, names.arg = dims,
  col = "steelblue", border = NA,
  xlab = "Number of Features",
  ylab = "Max Distance / Min Distance",
  main = "Curse of Dimensionality")
abline(h = 1, lty = 2, col = "red")
text(6, 1.3, "ratio → 1 means all distances are similar\n(KNN can't distinguish neighbors)",
     col = "red", cex = 0.8)
```
:::
